isch-flat.title: Ischemic Stroke: What Happens in the First 24 Hours
isch-flat.subtitle: CBF, OEF & the Penumbra
isch-flat.description: By 24 hours, blood flow at the center of an ischemic stroke drops below 20% of normal. Here's how it gets there, step by step.
points: How the brain compensates first: arteriolar dilation, rising OEF, CBV and MTT (Fig. 3.7)
Core vs rim: why flow falls most in the central territory and collaterals protect the edges
The timeline: CBF, CMRO₂ and OEF from 1 hour to 24 hours and beyond
The rim of high oxygen extraction, lasting up to 16 hours, and its variable fate
Spontaneous recanalization, luxury perfusion, and the chronic infarct
isch-flat.audience: For medical and pharmacy education: neurology, neuropharmacology and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), pp. 30–31, paraphrased. Graphs are schematic, after Fig. 3.7.
Music includes the Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0).
Educational content only, not medical advice.

cbf.title: Cerebral Autoregulation Explained: How the Brain Holds Its Blood Flow
cbf.subtitle: CPP, CVR & Carotid Stenosis
cbf.description: Between 70 and 150 mmHg of perfusion pressure, cerebral blood flow barely changes. Here's how the brain does it, and when it fails.
points: The autoregulation plateau: flow falls ≤ 18%, then steeply outside 70–150 mmHg
The lever: arteriolar diameter, cerebrovascular resistance (CVR), a ~10 s lag, and the rise in CBV
Myogenic vs metabolic control: why local oxygen wins in vivo
Chronic hypertension shifts the curve: lower limit 100–120 mmHg, and why that matters for ischemia
Local CPP, not MAP: CPP = MAP − ICP
Finite capacity: autoregulation lost in hypercapnia, anemia, hypoxemia
Carotid stenosis: no effect until 60–70%, and the role of collaterals
cbf.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: neurology, physiology, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), pp. 29–30, paraphrased. Curves are schematic.
Drums: "MuldjordKit" by Lars Muldjord (CC BY 4.0).
Educational content only, not medical advice.

thrombus-news.title: Thrombus Formation in 60 Seconds
thrombus-news.subtitle: Real Histology
thrombus-news.description: About three quarters of this clot is pale fibrin, and only a quarter red cells. Real microscope images show how a thrombus is built, and why that matters for clot-dissolving drugs.
points: A real clot cut open: layered bands of fibrin and red cells
Up close: the fibrin net that traps red cells (electron micrograph)
Fast arterial flow → platelet-rich clots; slow flow → fibrin-rich
The chain: tenase and prothrombinase on the platelet surface → thrombin → fibrin, cross-linked by factor XIIIa
t-PA and plasmin break fibrin down, and why fibrin content and cross-linking may affect how well clot-dissolving drugs work
thrombus-news.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: hematology, stroke, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), Ch. 2, "Thrombus formation", paraphrased.
Images: Mikael Häggström, M.D. (CC0); Janice Carr, CDC (public domain).
The 74% / 26% split is a colour count on one slide, an estimate (about ±3%), not a lab measurement.
Drums: "MuldjordKit" by Lars Muldjord (CC BY 4.0).
Educational content only, not medical advice.

thrombus.title: From Platelets to Plasmin: A Clot in 60 Seconds
thrombus.description: Inside a brain artery, a clot is built step by step, from the first platelets to the fibrin that holds it together, and the plasmin that can break it apart. Drawn in colored pencil.
points: Damaged lining: platelets stick first; in fast arterial flow, clots are platelet-rich
The platelet surface as a workbench: factors V and VIII speed thrombin generation
Thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin, the clot's scaffold
Factor XIII, switched on by thrombin, cross-links the strands
t-PA from the lining turns plasminogen into plasmin on the clot surface, and fragments can travel downstream
Why fibrin content and cross-linking may affect how well clot-dissolving drugs work
thrombus.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: hematology, stroke, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), Ch. 2, "Thrombus formation", and Fig. 2.2, paraphrased and redrawn. A teaching schematic, not to scale.
Educational content only, not medical advice.

two-roads-news.title: Two Roads to a Damaged Artery: How Cholesterol & Hypertension Drive Atherosclerosis
two-roads-news.subtitle: NOX2, Angiotensin II & ROS
two-roads-news.description: In this real human artery, one side of the wall is more than five times thicker than the other: 0.25 mm here, 1.36 mm there. What builds it? Two roads that meet in the same damaged wall.
points: A real human coronary artery section, measured: the thickening and its fat-laden cells
Road 1: high cholesterol → ↑ NOX2 oxidase → reactive oxygen species
Road 2: hypertension → angiotensin II → AT1 receptor → ↑ NADPH oxidases
Where they meet: ↓ nitric oxide, sticky white cells and platelets, inflammation → endothelial dysfunction
The mouse evidence: block either road (NOX2 or AT1R knockout) and most of the damage is blunted
two-roads-news.audience: Atherosclerosis underlies both coronary and cerebral artery disease. For medical and pharmacy students: cardiovascular and stroke pathophysiology, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), Ch. 1 and Fig. 1.1, paraphrased and redrawn.

Images: The GTEx Project, GTEX-13S86-0525, via NCI Imaging Data Commons (CC BY 4.0); "Lab mice" by Understanding Animal Research (CC BY 2.0, illustrative); "Blood pressure monitoring" by rawpixel.com (CC0).

deafness.title: Two Routes to the Cochlea: Types of Deafness Explained
deafness.description: Sound reaches the cochlea by two routes: through air and the ossicles, or through the bones of the skull. Every type of deafness, both tuning-fork tests, and the cochlear implant make sense once you know which route is broken.
points: Conduction deafness: a block in the outer or middle ear. Bone conduction still works, so it's never total.
Sensorineural deafness: damaged spiral-organ hair cells or cochlear nerve (e.g. acoustic neurinoma), so both routes fail
Weber test: fork on the mid-forehead; heard in the normal ear (nerve deafness) or louder in the affected ear (conduction deafness)
Rinne test: air vs bone; normally air > bone; bone > air in conduction deafness; both reduced in sensorineural loss
Cochlear implants: microphone → receiver under the skin → electrode array; each frequency activates its own electrodes, and patients relearn to hear
deafness.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: neuroscience, ENT, clinical examination, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Young PA, Young PH, Tolbert DL. Basic Clinical Neuroscience, 3rd ed. (Wolters Kluwer), pp. 165–168, paraphrased. Rinne results in hearing loss and the cochlea's frequency map are standard clinical teaching.
Drums: "MuldjordKit" by Lars Muldjord (CC BY 4.0).
Narration uses a synthetic voice.
